facts.claim: Weizenbaum’s ELIZA (1966) answered by keywords: each keyword came with rules that took a sentence apart and built the reply, and the keywords with their rules made up the bot’s script.
When no keyword turned up, Weizenbaum’s ELIZA (1966) fell back on a content-free remark or an earlier transformation, not an answer.
Apple introduced Siri with the iPhone 4S on October 4, 2011, as an assistant that helps you get things done just by asking.

Google’s Dialogflow docs (checked 2026-10-30): the default fallback intent is matched when the bot can’t match a user’s input to any other intent, and it answers with fixed lines such as “I didn't get that. Can you say it again?”

Sahami and colleagues (1998) trained a junk-mail filter on labelled messages: it sorted each message into junk or legitimate, and called it junk only when at least 99.9% sure, since losing real mail costs more.
Vaswani and colleagues introduced the Transformer in 2017, a network built on attention alone, dropping the building blocks earlier language networks relied on (recurrence and convolutions).
Brown et al. (2020) showed GPT-3, a model of 175 billion learned numbers, doing new tasks from a few worked examples placed in the prompt, with no further training.
Brown and colleagues posted the GPT-3 paper, “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners”, on May 28, 2020.

InstructGPT (Ouyang and colleagues, 2022) was made in three stages: fine-tuning GPT-3 on answers people wrote, collecting people’s rankings of the model’s outputs, then reinforcement learning from that human feedback.
In the InstructGPT paper, people preferred the answers of InstructGPT, with 1.3 billion learned numbers, to those of GPT-3, with 175 billion: a model about 100 times bigger.
OpenAI introduced ChatGPT on November 30, 2022, as a sibling of InstructGPT trained with the same human-feedback method, free to use during a research preview.
Ji and colleagues’ survey (ACM Computing Surveys, 2023) finds text-generating models prone to hallucinate: to produce content that is nonsensical or unfaithful to the source they were given.

In Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024 BCCRT 149), a British Columbia tribunal held Air Canada responsible for what the chatbot on its website told a customer: the chatbot is still part of the company’s website.
